articles.content_orig:
A suspect linked to a far-left movement has been arrested in France after a 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire over the weekend that broke out during mass disorder, French media report.
The clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall in the central city of Limoges were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.
The 34-year-old suspect is known to police for acts of violence against public officials and is on a French national security watchlist, FranceInfo and BFM TV report.
French Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu has vowed a "massive" police presence during further protests planned for Saturday, while several cities, including parts of Paris, will be subject to curfews this week.
Marseille mayor BenoÃ®t Payan said on X that the prefect had decided to introduce the curfew "starting this evening and for days to come", with French media reporting it would be in place overnight from Tuesday to Friday.
Payan said the measures apply to minors and will only be in commercial areas of the city, which were particularly affected by looting which took place last weekend.
Paris's police commissioner has also ordered the extension of an overnight curfew in the capital. The PrÃ©fecture de Police said the measure would continue "for as long as it proves necessary".
A curfew for parts of central Lyon was renewed on Tuesday, while overnight curfews for Nice and Lille are ongoing, and a week-long, overnight curfew for Bordeaux came into force on Tuesday night.
French Justice Minister GÃ©rald Darmanin told BFM Television that 149 people were in detention following widespread demonstrations over the weekend.
Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets to protest against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.
Darmanin previously said he asked prosecutors to be "extremely firm" and "ruthless towards those who attacked police officers, gendarmes and firefighters, who looted shops and who attacked public buildings".
Lecornu told French parliament on Tuesday afternoon a large number of police would meet demonstrators at a planned protest on Saturday.
Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez previously admitted police had "lost control" in some cities over the weekend.
He was strongly criticised by opposition politicians over authorities' preparedness for the disorder, leading him to offer his resignation on Monday, which was rejected by President Emmanuel Macron.
The city hall's roof and clock tower in Limoges was severely damaged in the fire
Lecornu also accused far-left groups of an "insurrectionary" plan over the weekend's mass chaos.
Responding to an earlier, similar accusation from Lecornu, left-wing La France Insoumise (LFI) de facto leader Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon had called for the prime minister to "prove his accusation" or "apologise, shut up, and stop stoking disorder".
On Tuesday, MÃ©lenchon urged followers on social media to show "restraint" in the face of any "provocation".
Lecornu earlier said targeted curfews introduced across France on Monday contributed to a quiet night following the disorder.
Curfews were introduced across parts of central Paris, including Place de la RÃ©publique, where protesters had gathered over the weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area.
Other measures restricting the movement of young people and gatherings were introduced on Monday in cities such as Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south, as well as Lille and other towns in the north.
A crowd assembled in Lyon on Monday night in support of businesses affected by the disorder but dispersed without violating the curfew, officials said.
The RhÃ´ne prefecture said on social media that it was "furious" that a far-right group tried to hijack the gathering. The prefecture said on X it reported the group to the public prosecutor for alleged Islamophobic and xenophobic remarks.
The streets in the southern city of Lyon were quiet on Monday night
Lecornu thanked police officers and gendarmes for enforcing the measures, adding that further curfews on Tuesday night would be decided depending on where they were necessary.
Writing in a post on X, he said decisions would be made "on the ground" by French regions and local mayors.
More than 2,500 people have been arrested since the disorder broke out, officials said on Monday. One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency. About 1,000 police officers were injured.
Protests first began last month with students demanding better school conditions but they have escalated to take in a broader range of concerns with numbers at demonstrations bolstered by trade unions and various protest groups.
Riots took place across French cities, including the capital Paris
More than 2,000 shops and other businesses have been directly impacted by the weekend's violence, the head of France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said.
Rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings and looting businesses in Paris, Marseille and other cities and smaller towns.
Protest organisers earlier declared that a second round of protests will take place on Saturday across France.
The so-called yellow vests (gilets jaunes), who were responsible for France's longest-ever modern protests in 2018, has said "Act II" will take place this weekend.
Meanwhile, French union La CGT has called for a major day of strikes on 5 November.

articles.title_orig: Women and children were main builders on batch of Terracotta Warriors: study
articles.title_zh: Women and children were main builders on batch of Terracotta Warriors: study
articles.content_orig:
Qin dynasty artisans included women and children assigned to pottery crafting, legal records and physical evidence show
Some 5 metres (16.4 feet) underground near one of China’s oldest cities lies the life-size army of thousands of terracotta warriors.
Now, a new study shows that a portion of the terracotta warriors was largely made by adult women and minors, not solely by men as previously thought.
“These findings challenge the long-held assumption that Terracotta Army production relied exclusively on adult male labour, providing the first quantitative biological evidence for a diverse workforce including women and children,” Shen Jingyi wrote in the paper published on October 13 in the peer-reviewed Journal of Cultural Heritage.

articles.title_orig: China, Russia Deepen Arctic Ties as Japan, Iceland Boost Science Cooperation
articles.title_zh: China, Russia Deepen Arctic Ties as Japan, Iceland Boost Science Cooperation
articles.content_orig:
(Stock image/Russian flag, from Pixabay)
Two senior fellows from the Sasakawa Peace Foundation, Natsuhiko Otsuka and Hiroyuki Enomoto, spoke at the Arctic Circle Assembly, held in Reykjavik, Iceland, from October 8 to 10.
Speaking on October 8, Otsuka highlighted growing cooperation between China and Russia to develop Arctic shipping routes and examined the broader international implications of a new Arctic cooperation framework proposed by Moscow.
On October 10, Enomoto discussed the growing collaboration between Japanese and Icelandic scientists in Arctic research. He also emphasized the importance of "science diplomacy" as the two countries mark the 70th anniversary of diplomatic relations.
Otsuka said China is "becoming a major power on the Arctic sea route," citing the rapid expansion of NewNew Shipping Line, a Chinese container shipping company established in 2022. Initially focused on shipping to Russia, the company has recently expanded its operations to include exports to Europe via the Arctic.
According to Otsuka, the company can afford the route's commercial risks because it expects "substantial cargo demand for Arctic shipping." One possible explanation is that its parent company handles shipments for both Chinese exporters and Chinese importers operating in Europe.
This gives NewNew Shipping Line an advantage, as it faces little price competition from major international shipping companies.
Japanese and South Korean shipping firms, however, face a different set of challenges. Given the geopolitical risks associated with Russia, Otsuka said it is not easy for carriers in either country to find domestic customers willing to ship goods along the Arctic route off Russia's northern coast.
On freight rates, Otsuka said the Arctic route would struggle to compete with the lower costs offered by ultra-large container ships passing through the Suez Canal.
Russia, meanwhile, faces significant challenges in developing the Arctic route. Its cargo volume targets are overly ambitious, while international isolation following its invasion of Ukraine has further complicated its plans.
Given these challenges, Otsuka said China's growing use of the route provides a much-needed boost to Russia's ambitions.
At an international conference hosted in September, Russia proposed a new framework for Arctic cooperation, seeking an alternative to the existing Arctic Council, whose seven other members continue to impose sanctions on Moscow.
Otsuka warned that the proposal could divide the region into two competing blocs: the "Arctic Seven" and a Russia-led group of sympathetic non-Arctic countries.
The Arctic Seven comprise the United States, Canada, Denmark, Iceland, Norway, Sweden, and Finland—all NATO members. Otsuka said the proposal could deepen tensions between NATO members in the Arctic and countries aligned with Russia.
For now, Otsuka described the prospect of establishing a new international body to rival the Arctic Council as being at an "uncertain conceptual stage."
However, he noted that growing cooperation between China and Russia on Arctic shipping is already producing tangible results. He suggested this cooperation could be a "practical step" toward establishing a new Russia-led international organization.
Speaking at a separate session, Enomoto thanked Icelandic government officials and university researchers for their contributions to growing scientific cooperation between Japan and Iceland.
Japan gained observer status on the Arctic Council in 2013 and has since strengthened its ties with Iceland through initiatives such as the Arctic Science Ministerial and the first Arctic Circle Tokyo Forum, held in 2023.
Iceland's ambassador to Japan, Hreinn Pálsson, echoed Enomoto's remarks, emphasizing the importance of science diplomacy in bilateral relations.
He also expressed hope that continued cooperation between Japanese and Icelandic scientists would help further strengthen ties between the two countries.

articles.title_orig: PHP2Shell: Two Unpatched Critical PHP RCE Flaws (CVSS 9.2) Trigger Emergency Security Alert
articles.title_zh: PHP2Shell: Two Unpatched Critical PHP RCE Flaws (CVSS 9.2) Trigger Emergency Security Alert
articles.content_orig:
This story is developing and was written before PHP's scheduled 14:00 UTC release on October 21. Once the release is out, the affected and fixed versions below are confirmed by the official advisory.
PHP will ship an out-of-cycle security release at 14:00 UTC today, October 21, for two critical vulnerabilities that its security team has rated 9.2 on the CVSS v4.0 scale but has not described.
Security researchers at watchTowr say the two flaws allow remote code execution. Only the four supported PHP branches, 8.2 through 8.5, can receive the fix, and no exploitation has been reported so far.
The advance notice followed a leak. On October 20, a post on HN said two PHP remote code execution flaws, rated CVSS 10.0 and affecting versions from PHP 5 onward, would be disclosed on Thursday, October 22. The poster said they had "no evidence beyond 'source: trust me, bro'".
watchTowr then posted on X that the leaked information was real, that the two flaws were under embargo, that everyone had been supposed to wait until Thursday, and that it could not share more for now.
PHP published its notice that evening, at 19:33 UTC, with the release set for Wednesday, a day before the date watchTowr gave. The notice says PHP may release earlier "should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild."
The leak carried the flaws' existence, a score, a date, and two CVE identifiers, not how the flaws work. The CVSS 10.0 figure is the leak's. PHP's rating is 9.2 on version 4.0 of the scale.
The identifiers researchers are using, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 , were also listed in the leaked post. PHP's notice names neither. The claim that every version since PHP 5 is affected is unconfirmed too: watchTowr's own FAQ on the flaws says that scope "has not been confirmed by an official vendor advisory" and that no configuration or feature requirement has been described.
PHP says "Full details, affected versions, and the fixed versions will be published with the release." Researchers have started calling the pair php2shell. The name is theirs, not PHP's.
Whatever the affected range turns out to be, PHP issues fixes only for its four supported branches , and records each branch's changes in its changelog . Versions 8.2 and 8.3 receive only security fixes, and 8.4 and 8.5 are in active support. Ahead of the release, several trackers, including Alpine Linux's and security researcher Kevin Beaumont, expect the fixes to ship as PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, the next point release of each branch, though PHP has not confirmed the numbers.
Anything older, including 8.1, 8.0, 7.x, and 5.x, is end of life and gets no PHP fix. If the flaws reach those branches, installations on them will have no vendor patch.
Security company Mallory counted about 884,000 internet-facing hosts whose HTTP banner reported a PHP version of 8.1 or older to the Shodan search engine on October 20, 59% of the roughly 1.5 million hosts that reported any version. The count covers banners, not confirmed affected systems, and a further 740,000 hosts reported PHP without a version.
PHP has published no workaround. Until the release lands, the preparation comes down to six steps, most of them drawn from a rapid-response post from Huntress , with CERT-EU's isolation advice added.
Huntress said it had not seen exploitation of the flaws in its partner environments as of October 20, had not built or reproduced a proof of concept, and was not aware of public exploit code. watchTowr's FAQ lists exploitation as none reported as of October 21 and the flaws as not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.
For comparison, when CVE-2024-4577 , a PHP flaw in CGI mode on Windows, became public in June 2024, Akamai saw exploit attempts against its honeypot servers within 24 hours.
The release should clarify what the notice withheld: which versions are affected, which part of PHP is involved, whether an attack requires a particular way of running PHP, a configuration, or a login, and how PHP itself describes the flaws. At the time of writing, PHP had not released the fixes.

articles.title_orig: China builds the world’s smallest wearable brain monitor with a cortex-wide view
articles.title_zh: China builds the world’s smallest wearable brain monitor with a cortex-wide view
articles.content_orig:
The Airscope offers a window on the simultaneous activity of thousands of individual neurons in untethered lab animals
Chinese scientists have developed what they say is the world’s smallest wearable mini brain monitor that can track the activity of thousands of neurons at the same time.
Weighing in at one gram (0.35 oz), the wireless “Airscope” is the lightest device of its kind and enables researchers to track a wider range of brain activity in untethered laboratory animals.
The device was jointly developed by scientists from Tsinghua University and the Chinese PLA Medical School, and detailed in a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Nature on Monday.
“This microscope will push optical brain-computer interfaces towards more precise neural detection,” said Dai Qionghai, the paper’s corresponding author from Tsinghua’s automation department.

articles.title_orig: China says it is 'safeguarding order' around Taiwan-controlled South China Sea atoll
articles.title_zh: China says it is 'safeguarding order' around Taiwan-controlled South China Sea atoll
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING, Oct 21 (Reuters) - China's government said on Wednesday that its coast guard was "safeguarding order" around a tiny and strategically located Taiwan-controlled atoll at the top end of the ‌South China Sea where Taipei fears Beijing is trying to enforce jurisdiction.
China, which views democratically governed ‌Taiwan as its own territory, said last week that Taiwan must "bear the consequences" of its coast guard using a water cannon ​against a Chinese fishing boat near the Pratas Islands.
Taiwan has reported two incidents since Sunday of Chinese coast guard vessels approaching the Pratas, accusing Beijing of provocative behaviour.
Speaking at a regular news briefing, a spokesperson for China's Taiwan Affairs Office said Beijing has "indisputable sovereignty" over the South China Sea islands, including the Pratas and ‌their adjacent waters.
"Mainland coast guard vessels conducting ⁠law enforcement patrols in the relevant waters are fulfilling their duties in accordance with the law, safeguarding normal navigation and operational order," spokesperson Zhang Han told reporters.
The ⁠Chinese ships are "effectively protecting the lawful and legitimate rights and interests of people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait and the safety of lives and property", she added.
The "obstinate insistence" by Taiwan's ruling party on its separatist ​stance is ​the root cause of the peril of war across ​the strait, Zhang said.
Taiwan's government rejects Beijing's ‌territorial claims, saying only the Taiwanese people can decide their future.
China recognises no claims of sovereignty by Taiwan and has never renounced the use of force to bring the island under its control.
The Pratas have no permanent civilian population and lie roughly between southern Taiwan and Hong Kong. Security experts see them as vulnerable to Chinese attack due to their distance — more than 400 km (250 miles) — from Taiwan.
China's military ‌already operates around Taiwan on an almost daily basis. Taipei has ​become increasingly alarmed by Beijing's use of its coast guard to ​carry out "law enforcement" patrols to try to ​assert jurisdiction.
Addressing a forum in Taipei late Tuesday, Taiwan's top China-policy maker said Beijing ‌is attempting to "domesticate" the Taiwan issue to "create an ​illusion of having de ​facto jurisdiction over Taiwan's surrounding waters and offshore islands".
With President Xi Jinping expected to be confirmed for a fourth term in office next year, China's mission to "achieve national unification" becomes even more ​pressing, said Chiu Chui-cheng, head of ‌the Mainland Affairs Council.
"We assess that Beijing's Taiwan policy will shift toward a more aggressive, ​provocative strategy of 'exercising jurisdiction before achieving unification'," he added.
(Reporting by Beijing newsroom; Additional reporting ​by Ben Blanchard in Taipei; Editing by Lincoln Feast.)

articles.title_orig: Scientists discover ghostly, eyeless creature hidden in Chinese cave
articles.title_zh: Scientists discover ghostly, eyeless creature hidden in Chinese cave
articles.content_orig:
A newly identified freshwater cave snail in China is offering scientists a rare glimpse into the little-known aquatic ecosystems hidden beneath East Asia. Published in the journal Subterranean Biology , the discovery represents an important step forward in understanding the region's underground wildlife. Until now, no freshwater cave snails had been documented in China, and the country's subterranean freshwater mollusks had received relatively little scientific attention.
The newly discovered species, Erhaia dijiang , has evolved remarkable features that allow it to live in complete darkness. As a true cave-dwelling animal, it has entirely lost its eyes, with the structures normally associated with vision having fully degenerated. The tiny snail also has a cone-shaped, nearly transparent shell, a delicate body without pigmentation, and long, slender tentacles.
Its unusual appearance inspired a name drawn from ancient Chinese mythology. Researchers chose dijiang in honor of "Di Jiang," a mountain patron god portrayed as a faceless beast in the ancient text Classic of Mountains and Seas (山海经). The connection is particularly fitting because the snail is extremely sensitive to light. During laboratory observations, individuals consistently retreated into dark spaces beneath rocks whenever they were exposed to illumination.
The location of the discovery is just as remarkable as the animal itself. Scientists found Erhaia dijiang at an elevation of 2,062 meters, making it the highest-altitude cave snail yet recorded within the family Erhaiidae. The finding demonstrates that freshwater cave snails can inhabit limestone cave systems at elevations above 2,000 meters.
Life in the Dark Waters of a Mountain Cave
Within its underground habitat, Erhaia dijiang lives among submerged gravel and broken rock in water less than one meter deep. The cave's water temperature stays close to 20°C, providing a relatively stable environment for the tiny mollusks.
Even when heavy seasonal rains increase the flow of water and occasionally wash a few snails out through the cave opening, they have not been observed in nearby streams. Researchers found that the animals remain confined to the cave environment, staying within two meters of its entrance.
Laboratory observations also provided clues about what these elusive creatures eat. The snails were seen feeding on diatoms, microscopic algae that grow on rock surfaces, and they also consumed fish food supplied by the researchers.
Only Three Living Snails Found, Raising Conservation Concerns
Although the discovery sheds new light on China's largely unexplored underground aquatic biodiversity, researchers are concerned about the species' future. They describe its conservation outlook as "far from optimistic."
During the first field investigation in August 2025, the team encountered an exceptionally small number of snails. Despite searching the shallow cave waters, researchers located only three living adults and one empty shell. They found no juveniles, suggesting that the known population is extremely sparse.
The scientists are now urging more comprehensive investigations of cave ecosystems throughout China to uncover additional species and better understand these fragile underground habitats. They also emphasize the need to develop conservation protections quickly for these vulnerable mollusks, which are native to highly restricted environments and could face serious threats before their populations are fully understood.

articles.title_orig: PHP warns it plans to release 2 emergency patches imminently
articles.title_zh: PHP warns it plans to release 2 emergency patches imminently
articles.content_orig:
Website admins, brace yourselves. Fixes for what are believed to be uncommonly severe vulnerabilities are scheduled to drop in a little more than 12 hours for PHP, a programming language that powers websites and Web applications everywhere.
PHP maintainers said Monday that they planned to release patches for two vulnerabilities, both with severity ratings of 9.2 out of a possible 10.
“All PHP users are encouraged to prepare now so they can upgrade as soon as the release is available,” the advisory stated. “We reserve the right to release earlier should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild.”
The maintainers published the advisory following the leaking of purported details, which have yet to be confirmed. The report showed a video of an exploit tool dubbed PHP2Shell executing code on webservers running WordPress 7.1.3, MediaWiki 1.46.2, phpBB 3.3.17, Magento 2.4.9, Joomla 6.2.0, Laravel 13.36.0, Laravel 8.83.29, Symphony 8.1.9, Drupal 11.4.10, and WHMCS 9.0.9, all of which use PHP. A video depicting the tool has been reposted here .
Attempts to locate the unconfirmed report were unsuccessful, but security firm watchTowr said it claimed to affect every PHP version from PHP 5, released in 2004, onward. The security firm went on to say it has confirmed that the vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, are real.
Researchers from separate security firm Sansec said they “expect mass attacks to start within 15 minutes of the release.” A third security firm, Webfence, also urged admins to prepare now. Huntress has also issued an advisory.
Preparation steps include identifying who is responsible for managing PHP inside an organization, taking an inventory of every app built on the language, planning a maintenance window starting at 14:00 UTC with contingency plans for earlier, making a backup of site and database files, and monitoring the PHP.net homepage for any late-breaking announcements, including an earlier release time. Some experts suggest unplugging any non-essential systems until they’re patched.
As an open source scripting language for building dynamic websites and web apps, PHP has come to be a de facto building block for the Web. It runs multiple CMS apps in addition to WordPress and also powers many internal tools. One security researcher said an estimated 1.3 million Internet-connected hosts are likely affected. Vulnerabilities with the severity the advisories are describing have the potential to inflict major damage across the Internet. Admins should remain aware that the patches can be released at any moment and remain vigilant until they do.

Based on the latest incentive data, our analysis found that the 2026 Toyota RAV4 can be a cheap upgrade over the Camry Hybrid despite having a higher MSRP. articles.content_orig:
OpenAI has revealed that agents operated by two of its most powerful models disabled their own safety monitoring when carrying out routine tasks, with one subsequently denying it had done so.
An agent powered by GPT Sol 6.1 disabled automatic alerts to OpenAI's security team, the company said in a blog post late on Tuesday. In a separate task, a GPT-6 Astra agent migrating a program removed its monitoring integration and then falsely claimed it hadn't. The incidents happened during internal coding tasks.
"In both cases, the agents considered whether monitoring safeguards should be preserved, but interpreted routine coding instructions as permission to weaken them," OpenAI said in a blog post.
Warnings about the risks of developing increasingly advanced AI systems have ramped up in recent months, amid cyberattacks from rogue models and growing calls for a slowdown from researchers building the tech.
The latest incidents reported by OpenAI highlight how agents can autonomously weaken safety guardrails while carrying out seemingly innocuous tasks.
OpenAI did not classify either incident under its most significant category, and the company said it was updating its misalignment monitoring system in response.

articles.content_orig:
While an IPAC report accurately notes that Britain is woefully unprepared to get relations with China right, the audit’s ideological framing is unhelpful
Getting relations with China right is widely seen as Britain’s epoch-defining challenge. It is also one it is woefully unprepared to face.
So concluded a recent audit by the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China (IPAC), which highlighted that top negotiators lacked basic Chinese language skills. More critically, it exposed a deeper deficit: a poor grasp of China spanning political elites and the public alike. This is rooted in a desk-bound classroom sinology rather than a nuanced appreciation and lived immersion.
Yet IPAC’s audit will do little to fix this deficit. Indeed, its ideological framing will deepen it.
The report depicts China as a neo-totalitarian state seeking to engineer the souls of its citizens. It alleges that this coercive ambition extends globally, that Beijing seeks to upend the liberal world order to usher in an era favourable to authoritarian imperialism.

articles.title_orig: Man, Woman Executed for 'Indecent Acts' in Mecca Mosque
articles.title_zh: Man, Woman Executed for 'Indecent Acts' in Mecca Mosque
articles.content_orig:
Bangladeshi authorities say they were not informed of the recent execution of two Bangladeshi nationals in the holy city of Mecca until after it had taken place, local media reports.
A Bangladeshi man and woman were executed last Wednesday after being convicted of committing an "indecent act" inside a mosque, according to the Saudi interior ministry. The ministry did not specify the nature of the offending act.
Bangladesh says it has reached out to the Saudi Arabian government to ask for more details about the case.
The two Muslim countries share a close relationship due to their religious affinity and strong economic ties.
More than three million Bangladeshis work and live in Saudi Arabia, mostly in low-paying jobs, and news of the double execution has raised public concern in Bangladesh.
According to the Saudi interior ministry, the two Bangladeshi nationals were convicted and sentenced to death under "tazir", which in Islamic law refers to punishments left to the discretion of the judge.
The ministry statement said they were handed the sentences because of the severity of the offence, and the fact that they violated the "sanctity" of the mosque.
Bangladesh has reached out to the Saudi government about the offences involved and legal proceedings in the case, said state minister for foreign affairs Shama Obaed Islam.
The government would consider next steps, such as the repatriation of the bodies, after getting information from Saudi authorities, Islam said.
She added that the government was committed to safeguarding the welfare and interests of Bangladeshis abroad.
The two executed Bangladeshis were included in a list of prisoners that Saudi Arabia had shared with Bangladesh, upon a request from the Bangladesh Consulate General in Jeddah - but that list did not indicate that the pair had been sentenced to death, the Daily Star reported.
This is not the first time that foreign nationals have been executed by Saudi authorities.
According to Amnesty International, the country has executed around 100 people this year, many of whom are foreigners convicted of drug offences.
In 2011, eight Bangladeshi men were publicly executed in the Saudi Arabian capital of Riyadh after they were found guilty of killing an Egyptian.
Earlier this month, Saudi Arabia overturned a death sentence handed to a Sri Lankan man over a comment he had made on Facebook, which had led to him being convicted of blasphemy. That decision came after the case sparked public outcry in Sri Lanka and spurred diplomatic efforts to seek clemency for the man.

articles.title_orig: France is divided over who to blame for weekend riots and what to learn from them
articles.title_zh: France is divided over who to blame for weekend riots and what to learn from them
articles.content_orig:
"This is not the face of France! You media all focus on the violence and destruction of Saturday's protests. But that's not the majority. It's not 'us'. That's not France!"
Elisabeth was speaking to me in front of a row of smashed shop windows, shattered glass still littering the tree-lined Parisian street. Its walls were daubed with red-lettered graffiti insulting French police and signed with the date of the riots, 17 October.
I'd stopped Elisabeth and her friend to ask their thoughts on what happened on Saturday. Elisabeth was so upset that, when she spoke, she seemed close to tears.
"My friend thinks this is civil war in France but I don't. Saturday is about something else entirely."
But what did happen exactly? Who was behind the riots? While much of the looting seemed opportunistic, the violence looked pre-planned. Why orchestrate it now, after weeks of student protests? And who most stands to gain from the destruction this weekend? Elisabeth wasn't entirely sure.
Different theories are doing the rounds - in and outside France. Black and white answers may be appealing, but the truth is there are many factors at play.
The president of the National Assembly, Yaël Braun-Pivet, has proposed a parliamentary inquiry into the riots and how they were organised.
French intelligence had briefed government circles earlier this month that left-wing anarchist groups were involved in the student protests. Their signature: a capital A, circled in black, was spray-painted on many buildings across France this weekend.
French media have played and replayed a video shot on Saturday showing groups of young men dressed in black, with a black, folded kerchief around their face to hide their identity, apparently attacking a number of police vans with what look like large hammers or machetes.
A French intelligence report dated 29 September, published by Le Figaro newspaper, details the "manipulation" of student demonstrations by student unions and political movements aligned with the radical left.
It suggests the far-left political movement La France Insoumise (LFI) was relying on violence as an electoral strategy ahead of the 2027 presidential elections. LFI denies this.
The mass looting of what is said to be over 3,000 shops and businesses on Saturday appears to have been largely opportunistic, according to French reports. Many youngsters immediately went online trying to sell their stolen wares, including designer trainers. Some didn't bother to cover their faces. Did they feel a sense of impunity?
Emmanuel Macron, who is on his way out as president and viewed by many in France as a lame duck, are accused of dropping the ball and failing to keep the country safe on Saturday.
Online sales platforms now say they'll work with the French authorities to track down as many of the looters as possible. Police say they're examining CCTV and social media footage. Macron insists all those responsible for violence or theft will be brought to justice.
Suggestions that some were encouraged to join in the violence by social media posts have led former Prime Minister Gabriel Attal (a hopeful in France's upcoming presidential election) to call for selected social media blackouts to quell further violence.
Belgium has also been experiencing violent protests these last days. On Tuesday, Belgium's interior minister, Bernard Quintin, warned of the "TikTokisation" of violence. Footage of riots is widely shared on social media, reaching a large audience of impressionable young people, he said, while also blaming violence on the streets of Brussels and Liège on "known far-left groups".
In France, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu and Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez have also clearly implicated the "hard left" in Saturday's mayhem - "pouring oil onto the fire", said Nuñez. On Tuesday Lecornu spoke of  "insurrections" planned by "small far-left and ultra-left groups".
Previously he had accused the "far left" of weaponising student demos.
It's something anti-capitalist LFI leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who also hopes to become French president, has vehemently denied.
Mélenchon took part in Saturday's planned protest. Politicians from his LFI movement have been present at the student demonstrations since they started a month ago in the socially deprived outskirts of Paris, with demands for better state education for all.
In Saint-Denis suburb on Monday, I met Lisa Cordat, of the FSE student union. She told me that students had organised themselves for demos via social media messaging or through student-led organisations. She said it was "insulting" to suggest they were being manipulated or "told to do this, or do that" by politicians.
"Student anger comes from the ground up," says Lisa.
But there is also a palpable frustration amongst many in France at what they see as the politicisation of Saturday's violence. Lina, who is 25, told me: "Politicians are hunting for scapegoats but don't ask why it all happened. The root causes of Saturday. We feel scared and abandoned."
France's leading politicians have indulged in a festival of finger-pointing since Saturday.
The presidential election here in six months' time is hotly contested and the volatility on French streets funneled immediately into France's already febrile politics.
Mélenchon, currently running in second place in most polls, ahead of centrist candidates, accused France's centrist prime minister of being "responsible for the chaos" either due to "incompetence or a worst-case strategy."
Mélenchon went on to apparently imply Lecornu may have allowed the violence to unfold, so as to position itself as a "party of order", after Saturday's lawlessness, "that would make people forget his failure in public finances".
France is struggling with spiralling public debt and government borrowing costs.
As for intelligence failures on Saturday, President Macron has demanded explanations and a new policing strategy. France's interior minister admitted there were not enough officers on the streets, despite the nationwide protests being publicised well in advance.
Following accusations of heavy-handedness at earlier demos, the police seemed very much out of their depth this weekend.
Of all the presidential hopefuls, it would seem Marine Le Pen of the anti-immigration National Rally party gains most politically from Saturday's shocking scenes.
She is already way ahead in opinion polls. Le Pen chose to launch a presidential-looking video address to the nation via social media on Sunday. Dressed formally, behind a large desk and in front of a French flag, she blamed Jean-Luc Mélenchon by name for his associates who "look to throw the country into chaos," she said.
She also accused the Macron government of "running out of steam", meaning that France was "taken hostage between violence and powerlessness".
She ended her video by reminding French voters they would have the opportunity to "choose a different path" in six months' time.
Le Pen's party promotes a law and order, closed-border message and, like US President Donald Trump and US Vice President JD Vance, has blamed migrants, amongst others, for the chaos in France on Saturday. French authorities have not implicated migrants in the violence.
One teacher called Mar complained that Saturday's violence "suits politicians' purpose. It distracts from weeks of legitimate protests for better public services", she said.
"Politicians aren't listening to what the students need, or what teachers need or what the French people want. They're using the violence to election-campaign to become president and to try to make their opponents look bad."
But increasing numbers in France, many amongst the young Gen Z generation, say they have dwindling faith in "the system".
That's something we see echoed in other European countries where mainly youth-led protests erupted - some violently - this weekend in Italy, Portugal and Albania as well as France and Belgium.

articles.title_orig: Alberta voters overwhelmingly reject separation process in a victory for Carney
articles.title_zh: Alberta voters overwhelmingly reject separation process in a victory for Carney
articles.content_orig:
The oil-rich province of Alberta has rejected the pathway to secession and will remain part of Canada, landing a definitive blow to a fringe but loud campaign which sought support from the US.
About three quarters of voters chose to stay in Canada, while one quarter opted to hold a second vote on separation later as of early Tuesday local time, with around 86% of polling locations reporting, according to unofficial results posted by the province.
Monday’s result comes amid a rising tide of patriotism and unity in Canada as the country has rallied against US President Donald Trump’s tariffs and annexation threats.
The Alberta independence campaign, a grassroots effort led by a handful of vocal separatists, was amplified heavily online, and some of its leaders had met with members of Trump’s administration.
The vote had faced concerns of possible foreign interference after Canadian newspaper the Globe and Mail reported Republican operatives had assisted top separatist leaders with their independence bid.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said the vote to remain means that “Albertans and all Canadians will move forward together with renewed purpose and high ambition” in a statement posted to X early Tuesday.
Thomas Lukaszuk, former Alberta politician and founder of the pro-unity Forever Canadian movement, said the result would send a strong message to Trump: “Canada is not up for grabs.”
“We are a solid country that’s united from coast to coast to coast and we stick up for each other,” Lukaszuk told a cheering crowd as the results came in.
The morning after the vote, leading separatist activist Jeffrey Rath told CNN that he was proud that his movement managed to convince roughly a quarter of voters to ask for a referendum.
“We started basically from nothing, a year and a half ago, and we’ve dominated the conversation,” Rath said. “For a fledgling political movement, it was a major victory and a hell of an accomplishment.”
At least one separatist group has not yet acknowledged the loss of the referendum side. The Alberta Prosperity Project, which organized a petition drive for an independence vote earlier this year, said in a statement on X that it awaits “the release of the official count and a careful analysis of the process before drawing conclusions.”
“This isn’t over, Alberta,” the organization added.
Monday’s vote was the first plebiscite of its kind in Canada since the 1995 Quebec referendum, where the predominantly French-speaking province voted against secession by a razor thin margin.
Alberta, a province roughly the size of Texas, has long harbored a fringe independence movement. Separatists there argue that Canada’s federal system underrepresents its population of 5 million in parliament, that Canadian efforts to fight climate change threaten Alberta’s lucrative fossil fuel industry and that Alberta’s conservative politics are often outweighed by the more liberal eastern provinces.
Though separation frequently polled low in Alberta, the movement grew louder after Carney’s Liberal Party won the 2025 federal elections amid a trade war with the United States.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced in May the province would hold a referendum on whether to remain in Canada, or to have a “binding provincial referendum” on independence later.
Over the past two years, secessionist leaders have met with US officials in Washington to try and negotiate support from the Trump administration. Rath, who was part of the group in DC, told CNN last year that Trump’s election in 2024 gave independence activists hope.
“If anybody is going to have the guts to recognize an independent Alberta, (it) would be the Trump administration,” Rath said.
News of the meetings at the time incensed Canadian politicians , who accused separatist leaders of “treason.”
The movement also possesses a Trumpian flavor. Participants at a secessionist rally CNN attended in 2025 donned red MAGA-style “Make Alberta Great Again” hats. A minority even said that Alberta ought to skip independence and become the 51st US state.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has lent support to the separatist cause, saying Albertans are “very independent people” and that the province is a “natural partner for the US” in an interview earlier this year.
Last week, Elon Musk, a Trump ally, urged Alberta, along with other Canadian provinces Saskatchewan and Quebec to separate from Canada in a post to his platform X, saying they would be “better off.”
Smith said she was “very pleased” with the result to remain in Canada in a post to X late Monday local time, but she has previously cautioned against “demonizing” independence supporters.
“We have had, from time to time, these kinds of initiatives flare up,” Smith told CNN in 2025. “And they’re almost always in response to a federal government that’s out of control. But they have all subsided when the federal government got back in its own lane.”
Carney, who grew up in Alberta, nodded to that frustration in a speech in Calgary last week urging voters to reject secession. “The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real,” Carney said.
But, the prime minister said, separation would only “burden” Albertans “with years of deep division and great uncertainty.”
He also made an oblique swipe at the US.
“This referendum comes at the worst possible time,” he said. “The world has become more dangerous and divided. Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us.”

articles.title_orig: 296 km/h: Super Typhoon Champi is now the strongest storm on Earth in 2026
articles.title_zh: 296 km/h: Super Typhoon Champi is now the strongest storm on Earth in 2026
articles.content_orig:
Super Typhoon Champi has now grown into the world’s strongest tropical cyclone of 2026, with respect to wind speed.
The system in the western Pacific Ocean became a powerhouse with its peak winds of of 296 km/h, the equivalent of a Category 5 storm.
Hurricane Polo previously held the title for world’s strongest tropical cyclone in 2026, in terms of wind speed. The storm peaked with maximum, sustained winds of 285 km/h and a minimum, central pressure of 892 mb--which is still lower than Champi's (895 mb)--making Polo stronger in that regard.
Such a low air pressure made Polo the second-most intense hurricane on record in the eastern Pacific.
Champi is also now the world’s seventh Category 5 storm of the year.

The typhoon also had a very healthy structure on radar as it passed Guam early Sunday morning local time.
Sea surface temperatures in this section of the western Pacific are running around 30°C , which is slightly warmer than normal for this time of year. The environment around the typhoon features deep moisture, calm winds, low wind shear. and enough upper-level support to vent air away from the storm.
The massive Champi will continue to track west towards Taipei before turning northwest later this week.
It will enter a more unfavourable environment, so Champi is forecast to weaken to a Category 4 or 3 storm by Thursday and Friday.
All of those ingredients, plus the storm’s own internal organization, are critical for a tropical cyclone to maintain its composure and continue strengthening.
The massive storm is tugging on the jet stream, having an influence on weather patterns across the globe.
Champi took a more westerly track towards Taiwan. Downstream, impacts to Canada are expected , reinforcing an end-of-October and early-November pattern we have previously been forecasting.
In Ontario and Quebec, the weather is expected to become more changeable and unsettled at times during the middle of and late next week, lingering into the following week.
Warmer-than-normal temperatures are expected to dominate, but quick interruptions are also expected.

articles.title_zh: Americans who moved to Europe after Trump win now say they regret leaving
articles.content_orig:
FILE: People walk past an American flag at the start of a work day, at the Oculus, part of the World Trade Center transportation hub in New York, Sept. 11, 2019. (AP Photo/Wong Maye-E, File)
Liberal Americans who fled to Europe after President Donald Trump 's re-election shared how the grass is not always greener on the other side of the Atlantic Ocean.
Wired Magazine released an article Thursday headlined "They Fled Trump’s America. Now They Regret It," speaking directly to those who sought "political refuge in the wake of Trump’s second term," but have since voiced frustration with Europe’s lower quality of life, the rise of right-wing politics in those countries, and a newfound appreciation for the cultural norms and niceties of American life.
One account, from a woman nicknamed "Annie," said she was sold the idea of an idyllic U.K. life on social media, "But the reality of life in the U.K. was dramatically different to what she’d imagined ."
"There are huge misconceptions about access to quality healthcare, standard of living… the quality of life is significantly lower than in the U.S.," she told the magazine, citing challenges ranging from their healthcare system to a significantly lower disposable income. "Things in the U.K. that are considered luxury items are very common" in America, like a dishwasher and dryer, she told Wired.
FRENCH AI CEO WARNS AMERICANS AGAINST VOTING DEMOCRAT, SAYING 'YOU DON'T WANT TO BE FRANCE'
Many expats noted that they grew to appreciate American values and culture after they tried living in Europe. (iStock)
Annie told the outlet that despite believing she'd have free healthcare under the NHS, she now pays "huge amounts of taxes and an immigration surcharge" to access the national healthcare services.
"So no, the health care is not free here," she said.
Annie was also surprised by the amount of anti-American hostility she experienced and cultural differences in the workplace.
"I found it particularly surprising how people feel so comfortable mocking my accent and culture, even in a workplace environment," she said. "The U.K. is very much a place of ‘it is what it is,’ but as Americans we are taught to always improve and strive for better things."
"I thought that ‘British politeness’ existed as it does in movies," Annie added, "but unfortunately, the reality is that present-day British culture is very individualistic, as well as without the sense of charity and helpfulness that many parts of American culture value."
WORLD CUP SOCCER FANS ARE DISCOVERING AMERICA’S GREATNESS. IT’S TIME AMERICANS DID, TOO
"I thought that ‘British politeness’ existed as it does in movies," one woman told Wired Magazine, "but unfortunately, the reality is that present-day British culture is very individualistic, as well as without the sense of charity and helpfulness that many parts of American culture value." Sarah Wood González, a journalist and consultant, made similar comments about learning to appreciate the American mindset and work culture once she was in a different environment.
"Something I had taken for granted is the American outgoingness and default to action, where the question is ‘how can we collaborate?’" she said. "Generally speaking, I also found that the American work style, for better or for worse, moves much faster and can get to a yes or no in less time."
"Finding work was so hard, and the endless bureaucracy had grown worse since I’d left," Josh, who moved to Germany, told Wired. "I missed the friendlier people, freedom of speech, and ease of daily life" in the United States, he said. He added of German daily life, "If you aren’t born and raised there, and don’t look German, you’ll never be fully accepted."
Josh told the magazine he moved back to the U.S. recently and is much happier. He admitted he may have "overreacted" by fleeing to Europe.
Many Americans who shared their regrets on social media were berated by fellow liberals for wanting to move back to "evil" America, the article also said.
"These posts are usually met with a huge amount of backlash. Commenters are quick to imply that the poster must be right-wing and privileged, in for a nasty shock if they did return home," Wired Magazine summarized. "Ironically, many times, they parrot the right-wing notion that they probably aren’t trying hard enough to assimilate into their new country. When one person recently said they badly missed their community of friends in a 'blue city in a blue state' and were considering moving back, the majority of top comments agreed the user was 'insane.'"
Protesters with the activist group Refuse Fascism demonstrate against President Donald Trump outside the White House in Washington, Monday, Nov. 17, 2025. ( Heather Diehl/Getty Images)
Daniel Di Martino, a Manhattan Institute fellow and economist who was born in Venezuela, spoke to Fox News Digital about how some misguided Americans tend to have unrealistic notions about European life.
"Things aren’t always great in Europe, but Europe is not one thing. Living in Greece, making the average salary of a Greek person, would be considered near poverty level in America. Living in Denmark, like an average Dane, is definitely fine, but they still earn much less than the average American," he said. articles.title_orig: Nigeria confirms Ebola case as outbreak spreads into western Africa
articles.title_zh: Nigeria confirms Ebola case as outbreak spreads into western Africa
articles.content_orig:
Case in Africa’s most populous country was detected in a woman who had travelled from Uganda
Nigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the health ministry said.
The woman began showing symptoms on 7 October and was admitted to a hospital in Abuja four days later, where she was later diagnosed with Ebola. It is unclear when she arrived in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country.
The health minister, Muhammad Pate, said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient. “We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all the contacts the individual may have had,” he said.
Uganda’s ministry of health said the patient had only transited through Uganda and that she is a Nigerian woman who had been on a business trip to Congo’s eastern region. The Nigerian authorities have not disclosed her nationality.
“Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation,” the ministry said in a statement. The ministry insisted Uganda has “no confirmed active Ebola cases”.
Nigeria is the latest country to report an Ebola case as the outbreak spreads across the region. Kenya confirmed its first case earlier this month and has since recorded nine infections. Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases, but it later declared itself free of the virus.
Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centers for Disease Control, said on X that “we are facing an extremely serious threat,” with a fatality rate of nearly 50% of cases.
“This Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak has already become the most geographically extensive in history, affecting several countries spread across three regions of Africa,” he said.
The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control said two weeks ago it was stepping up surveillance following the detection of Ebola in Kenya and strengthening the country’s preparedness for a potential outbreak.
“These efforts have focused on early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, risk communication and protection of health care workers,” the agency said.
Nigeria established an Ebola taskforce in June after the outbreak in Congo in mid-May.
The spread of Ebola beyond Congo has heightened fears among health authorities about the rapid transmission of the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has infected more than 9,500 people and killed more than 4,600 people.
The latest Ebola outbreak is the fastest-spreading on record and is on track to exceed the deadliest on record, the 11,000 people killed in West Africa’s regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016, WHO has said.

articles.title_orig: Boeing 737 MAX 10 lands long-awaited FAA certification
articles.title_zh: Boeing 737 MAX 10 lands long-awaited FAA certification
articles.content_orig:
Nearly a decade after Boeing unveiled its largest 737 Max jet, the company has cleared a major hurdle in its effort to bring the plane to airlines. The Federal Aviation Administration approved the Max 10 for passenger service Tuesday, ending years of delays.
The 737 Max 10’s certification represents another milestone in Boeing’s efforts to restore its reputation and financial footing after years of safety, quality and production challenges. With production approved, the aircraft can now be sold to domestic and foreign carriers.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the certification followed “extensive safety reviews,” including thousands of hours of test flights, and called it a major win for American manufacturing.
“To think that it took us almost 10 years to get here. We all probably had a little less gray hair 10 years ago," Duffy said during a visit to Boeing's manufacturing plant Tuesday in Everett, Washington.
The Max 10 is an important piece of the company's effort to regain ground in the narrow-body market. For airlines, the larger plane offers a way to carry more passengers on a single flight, potentially lowering costs per seat. For travelers, it could eventually mean more seats on popular routes, though the impact on fares will depend on how airlines deploy the planes and how much competition they face.
Stephanie Pope, president and CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes, said during Duffy's visit that the certification "clears the path to deliver an airplane that will set a new standard in commercial aviation." The Max 10 will typically seat 185-210 passengers, according to Boeing, compared with 175-195 on the Max 9 and 160-180 on the Max 8.
“Today is a very, very special day. It caps years of hard work and dedication by many," Pope said. "It marks another major milestone in our recovery, and it unlocks a key to our future growth.”
The company expects to begin deliveries in 2027.
The single-aisle jet was introduced at the Paris air show in 2017 to help Boeing compete with rival Airbus. But technical and regulatory hurdles repeatedly delayed certification.
Boeing’s struggles have been particularly acute since two deadly crashes involving the smaller Max 8 killed 346 people in 2018 and 2019 off the coast of Indonesia and in Ethiopia. In 2024, a panel flew off of an Alaska Airlines Max 9 in midair, renewing scrutiny of Boeing’s manufacturing and safety practices.
The delays have held up a key part of Boeing's business. More than 30 customers worldwide have ordered 1,555 Max 10s that Boeing has yet to deliver, accounting for more than 30% of its total 737 Max backlog.
Major customers include United Airlines, Delta Air Lines, American Airlines and Ryanair. Alaska Airlines joined that list in January, ordering 105 Max 10s, with options for 35 more.
The Max 10 is intended to compete with Airbus’s A321neo model family, which entered service in 2017. The largest A321neo can carry more passengers and fly farther without refueling than the Max 10.
Still, Boeing designed the Max 10 to carry more passengers while burning less fuel than older aircraft — a potentially attractive combination for airlines facing soaring jet fuel costs amid the U.S. war with Iran. Those rising costs have put added pressure on airlines to control expenses.
Certification means the FAA has determined that the Max 10’s design meets safety standards, following engineering reviews and flight testing. But Boeing must continue to show it can consistently build the aircraft to the approved design, and each plane must be cleared before it can fly passengers.
The Max 10’s certification completes the lineup of four 737 Max models. The FAA cleared the Max 7 for airline operations in August.
Pope on Tuesday described the certification of both the Max 7 and Max 10 in the same year as a sign of the company’s resilience.
In the wake of the fatal Max 8 crashes, the FAA overhauled how it certifies Boeing aircraft. But over the past 18 months, the agency has gradually eased some of its restrictions on the company, increasing the limit on how many planes Boeing can produce. In July, the FAA also said Boeing could once again issue airworthiness certificates for its 737 Max and 787 planes at the end of production, allowing the company to take back some responsibility for determining whether finished aircraft are ready to fly.

articles.title_orig: Japan exports post huge miss in September as growth slows to 16.7%
articles.title_zh: Japan exports post huge miss in September as growth slows to 16.7%
articles.content_orig:
Japan's exports in September rose 16.7% from a year earlier, missing market expectations by a huge margin. Reuters-polled analysts had pegged exports growth at 20.1%.
This is the second straight month that shipments from Japan have recorded a slowdown, after hitting a near four-year high in July.
Growth was supported by continued strong semiconductor exports, with shipments rising 49.4% year on year by value.
Exports of machinery also bolstered growth, with semiconductor-related machinery shipments up 43.9% and power generation machinery exports climbing 22.6%.
In terms of destinations, shipments to mainland China — Japan's largest trading partner — rose 8.6%, while exports to the U.S. climbed 22.9%. Exports have been the main driver of Japan's growth for the first two quarters of 2026, helping the world's fourth largest economy beat expectations in the first quarter, and supporting growth in the second.
Japan's imports in September grew 18.9%, also missing expectations of 19.6% from Reuters.
Tokyo's imports of petroleum climbed 51.1% by value in September, with inbound shipments from the U.S. surging nearly 820%, while those from the Middle East inching up just 1.5% as the conflict in the region continues to impede supplies.
Following the data release, the benchmark Nikkei 225 was up 1.8%, while the Topix gained 1.14%.
The data comes as the Bank of Japan is set to meet next week, and Reuters poll estimates indicate that the central bank is set to hold its policy rate steady at 1%.

articles.title_orig: Borneo burning: Life on the frontline of South East Asia's toxic haze
articles.title_zh: Borneo burning: Life on the frontline of South East Asia's toxic haze
articles.content_orig:
When the sun hits the smog enveloping Indonesian Borneo, it turns everything the colour of rust. Cars, houses and streets appear and disappear out of a dim russet fog. There are few better words than "apocalyptic" to describe the way this looks.
But it's at night, in the quiet darkness, that mother-of-three Dianyra Eka Nastiti grows most fearful.
"Sometimes at night my baby's chest makes a rattling sound," she says. "She was hospitalised for bronchopneumonia when she was just a month and a half old, and every single night I worry: Will my child cough tomorrow?
"Those thoughts haunt me every night."
Nastiti lives in Palangkaraya, at the frontline of a months-long environmental catastrophe that has blanketed large parts of Southeast Asia in a toxic haze.
Wildfires have torched some 1.9 million hectares across Indonesia since the start of the year, according to open-access satellite platform Nusantara Atlas – an area roughly the size of the US state of New Jersey, or the entire landmass of Fiji. One million hectares are thought to have burned in September alone.
But the toxic fallout is larger still. Swathes of smouldering forest, swamp and peatlands have turned the air thick with microparticles and carbon monoxide, creating a noxious cloud that has swaddled Indonesia and drifted as far as Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines.
As of mid-October, Indonesia's Health Ministry had recorded more than 277,000 cases of people suffering from chronic coughs and acute respiratory infections. More than 62,000 of those were infants and toddlers under the age of five.
"The forest fires have had a huge impact, especially on everyone's health," says 22-year-old Natari Victoria, who was admitted to a health centre in Palangkarya after suffering from a cough for more than a week.
"I have young cousins, including babies, who are coughing too. It's really taking a toll on them."
Haze and smoke from peat fires contain a complex mixture of pollutants that pose serious health risks to the human body.
Among these are tiny microparticles which can penetrate deep into the lungs and, in some cases, enter the bloodstream, causing inflammation, chronic lung diseases and increased risk of premature death.
Another concern is the toxic greenhouse gases that are being unleashed into the air.
"Here in Central Kalimantan, especially in Palangkaraya, the sky has turned yellow and hazy," says Riduan, head of the Palangkaraya Health Office. "So what are the residents actually breathing in? It's not fresh oxygen; it's carbon dioxide and pollutants. And what happens as a result? The body – specifically the brain – doesn't get enough oxygen."
Children, older adults and pregnant women are particularly vulnerable to the dangers of haze, especially during prolonged periods of exposure, when the health impacts can accumulate.
In places like Palangkarya, the official advice is to stay indoors and avoid going out. But Nastiti says this is unrealistic.
"I still need to buy vegetables, stock up on food, purchase school supplies, and take care of other necessities," she explains. "It's simply not possible, and I feel like the people who say things like that have no idea what is actually happening here."
Nastiti's utmost priority, however, is the health and wellbeing of her children. And when the haze grows heavy, she is quick to force them inside.
"With conditions being so unsafe, I have no choice," she says. "Our young children should be at the park, playing with their friends and going to school. Instead, they are locked inside the house."
Lola Macitri, a 37-year-old who lives in the rural village of Ramang, 50km (31 miles) north of Palangkaraya, has been similarly housebound. As the smog has deepened over the past few weeks – from dusty grey to amber yellow and, more recently, burnt orange – she and her family have come to spend most of their time indoors.
Her children, like many others in Indonesia's more haze-affected areas, have been doing their school classes online, she says, while she and other adults struggle to manage half-a-day's work out in the poisonous air.
Countless farmers, daily-wage earners and small vendors have similarly been forced to either sacrifice their livelihoods or endure the risk of stepping outside. Beyond that, many are left with no choice but to wait out the storm.
"If you ask whether we are afraid of the health risks, of course we are. But where else can we go?" says Macitri. "We just have to endure and stay strong through this situation, because there is simply no other option."
The government is under mounting pressure from the public to do more to stop the fires, with many criticising what they see as a woefully inadequate response by the authorities.
Authorities insist they have pursued a range of measures to try to extinguish the flames and, in turn, the smoke – from aerial waterbombing to experimental weather modification. Last week, the Indonesian government said it had deployed more than 60,000 personnel to carry out a "land operation", claiming they'd achieved an 80% success rate in extinguishing new fires.
"At this point, I think we need to use every safe and effective option available to suppress the fires," says Dr Nisa Novita, a forestry expert and peatland researcher at Indonesian conservation NGO Yayasan Konservasi Alam Nusantara (YKAN).
"It's a bit like trying to save a sinking ship: we need to act urgently, use whatever tools can help, and prevent further damage while we still can."
But those resources are fast depleting for responders on the ground.
For more than 100 days, Juni has been fighting wildfires that show only false signs of abating. On the surface, the flames are out – but underground, smouldering blazes continue to burn through a deep understory of carbon, vegetation and peat.
"It is truly exhausting," he says, describing how the relentless smoke has produced in him a shortness of breath, a persistent cough and an unshakeable pain in his eyes. When asked what he needs, he says "air".
"The haze makes it hard to breathe," he explains. "We are just hoping for heavy rain."
Thousands of others across Indonesia and Southeast Asia have spent the past several months hoping for the same.
Seasonal wildfires are not new to Indonesia but this year, a so-called Super El Nino has amplified drought conditions and delayed the kind of rainfall that is critical to extinguishing peat fires. It has also made things exponentially harder for those at the coalface, like Juni, who have spent months battling a seemingly irrepressible fire front.
Dr Novita explains that conditions on the ground have become much harsher even in recent weeks, as the prolonged drought makes water increasingly scarce.
Fauzi Rahman, another firefighter in Palangkaraya, highlighted this as one of the main difficulties confronting him and his peers.
"Peatland fires are hard to put out because they require a lot of water and a long time," he says. "On regular land we can clear 20 hectares in a single day, especially with a large team... On peatland, it can take months.
"We really have to inject water deep down, all the way to the bottom, which requires a huge amount of water. And right now, water is hard to find."
What's more concerning for Dr Novita, however, is that her team has reported fires spreading into areas where there has been no history of fire before.
"So we're not only dealing with fires in the usual hotspots but also seeing them emerge in new areas," she says.
In Palangkaraya, people are growing desperate for an end to this apocalypse. But it will likely take a force of nature for that to happen any time soon.
Riduan, head of the Palangkaraya Health Office, tells the BBC that "hopefully, with all the extraordinary efforts from the community, the military, and the police working together, the fires can be put out".
"However, as of right now, the fires are still burning," he adds. "So what can we hope for? Our greatest hope is that Almighty God will bring us rain soon."

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose on Tuesday as a number of upbeat earnings reports and a drop in oil prices overshadowed recent pressure seen among artificial intelligence-related stocks.
The blue-chip index gained 529.85 points, or 1.02%, to end at 52,495.88, while the S&P 500 added 0.28% and closed at 7,712.57. The Nasdaq Composite inched down 0.02% to 26,424.82.
Shares of industrial and safety products producer 3M offered a boost to the Dow, jumping more than 5% following better-than-expected earnings results and a full-year guidance raise . Shares of aerospace and defense company Northrop Grumman advanced more than 4% after it posted an earnings beat.
Meanwhile, oil prices pulled back from earlier gains, helping investor sentiment. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures fell 1.8% to settle at $101.79, while Brent crude futures declined 0.7% to $108.79 a barrel. The moves in oil, which added to the declines in Treasury yields , come as traders continued to monitor developments in the Middle East.
The market has been weighed down as of late by worries about the sustainability of the AI trade amid debt and demand concerns. In fact, sentiment in tech took a hit earlier in the day after Korean AI firm Elice tumbled more than 30% overnight in its public market debut. Asia-Pacific markets declined Tuesday, after U.S. stocks rose overnight, leading to declines in the South Korean market.
However, some AI-related stocks staged a bit of a comeback as the session went on. Western Digital gained more than 3%, while Seagate Technology was up more than 2%. CoreWeave and Marvell Technology each advanced more than 1%.
The S&P 500 finished in positive territory on Monday, while the Nasdaq Composite advanced more than 1%. That marked a rebound from last week's rout, when anxieties around companies borrowing too much money for their AI build-outs intensified.
"For much of this year, the market has been willing to look through higher rates because the growth story, notably that around AI, was strong enough to justify it. Last week, we saw that relationship begin to be tested," said Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion.
"Hyperscalers report over the next few weeks, setting up the next major stress test for the AI trade," he continued. "Guidance around ROI, data center spending and 2027 capex will arguably be more important than the headline earnings figures."
